excerpt: November 25, 2026 Why is LLM inference hard? When I first heard about inference engines, like vLLM, I wondered what makes inference so challenging. That’s why I decided to learn more about LLM inference from a systems perspective. If you already know how transformers work, then this is a fun topic to explore. In case you don’t, I recommend watching this awesome YouTube video by 3Blue1Brown. In this blog post you’ll learn about KV cache, paged attention, continuous batching and flash attention. Let’s get started! Attention Revisited Let’s briefly recap what happens in the attention layer when an LLM is prompted with something like “Edsger Dijkstra was a dutch computer scientist who”. First, the keys and the queries are calculated from token embeddings and the attention scores are derived as follows: For simplicity, we consider only a single head. The first forward pass, called prefill, processes the whole prompt at once and fills in the entire attention matrix. From then on, in the decode phase, each new token adds just a single row. We now know how much “made” attends to each earlier token, we use these scores to take a weighted sum of the value vectors, and update the embedding for “made”. With attention revisited, let’s take a look at some of the systems challenged involved. KV cache LLMs generate one token at a time. At every decode step, the keys and the values of all earlier tokens, whether they came from the prompt or were generated, are exactly the same as in the previous step. Recomputing them would be wasted work. So inference engines compute them once, store them, and reuse them in every later step. This is the KV cache. But LLMs don’t know in advance how many tokens they will generate when prompted. How are we gonna know the amount of space needed for the KV cache in that case?
